nodes.body:
Fixes #1193.

## Problem

Since 648c6848 ("Remove unnecessary embedded environment from FnPtr"), a closure gets its environment only from its function's entry in the lib, which closures of the main script don't have. A closure kept by the host and called after the script has finished, with `FnPtr::call`, no longer finds the script's `import`s:

```rust
import "m" as m; keep(|| m::who());
```

fails with `ErrorModuleNotFound("m")` when the kept closure is called. It worked in 1.26.1. The bisect and the repro are in the issue.

## Changes

**Commit 1: AST walker.** Put back `FnPtr::env`, set when a closure literal is evaluated (as before 648c6848), and prefer it to the lib's environment when calling. The bare function name as a variable (6f4ed21f) keeps `env: None`, so the fix for a module's closure seeing the caller's functions stays. `FnPtr` is 48 bytes again. Test: `test_module_closure_keeps_imports`.

**Commit 2: Grain.** The first commit left Grain unchanged, and it hit the same error: the compiler pools closure literals as constants and the VM pushed them with `env: None`.

- The VM now gives a loaded `FnPtr` constant an environment built from its global state, as `get_literal_value` does for the walker. It checks only when the program uses function pointers (`Caps::FN_PTR`), so other programs pay one flag test per constant load.
- `constant_caps` refuses a `FnPtr` that already has an environment, so such a constant is not pooled. The compiler leaves it to the walker instead of writing an artifact that loses the environment and fails the same way when read back. (As suggested in the issue discussion.) I could not get an `env: Some` constant into an AST through the public API, since the optimizer rebuilds scope-constant closures as `Fn("anon$…")` calls, so this guard is defensive.
- Tests: a Grain version of the repro (`a_kept_closure_keeps_the_imports_of_its_script`) and a unit test for `constant_caps`.

## Design note

I did not fragment every closure literal into a residual so that the walker sets the environment. That would stop `a.map(|x| ..)` and similar from lowering, and the Grain `AGENTS.md` says to prefer instructions over fragments. Setting the environment in the VM needs no new opcode and no wire-format change.

## Testing

`cargo test --tests` passes with the default features, `internals,grain`, `bin-features,grain,internals`, and `internals,grain` combined with each of `no_closure`, `no_function`, `no_module` and `no_object,no_index`. The library builds without warnings under several `no_*` combinations.

Fixes the `NoStdBuild` jobs, which have been red on every branch since the nightly of 2026-10-16 (seen on #1189 and #1190, which touch nothing `no_std`-specific; `main`'s run of 2026-10-13 was still green).

rust-lang/rust#148413 (merged 2026-10-15) mangles the personality symbol like the other std-internal symbols, so the pre-built `core`/`alloc` now reference `__rustc::rust_eh_personality`, and the `#[no_mangle] extern "C" fn rust_eh_personality()` in `no_std/no_std_test/src/main.rs` no longer satisfies the linker:

```
error: linking with `cc` failed: exit status: 1
  = note: Undefined symbols for architecture arm64:
            "__RNvCs6EUDi8WbMwz_7___rustc19rust_eh_personality", referenced from: ...
```

The change declares the function as `#[lang = "eh_personality"]` (with `#![feature(lang_items)]`), which is what rust-lang/rust's own `no_std` binary fixture (`tests/run-make/no-alloc-shim/foo.rs`) moved to in that PR. The compiler then emits the symbol under whatever name it expects, so the harness builds on nightlies before and after the change. The routine is still never called, since every profile sets `panic = "abort"`; the other shims are untouched.

Verified locally on aarch64-apple-darwin: with `nightly-2026-10-16` the harness fails to link without this change and builds with it, for `--profile unix` and `--profile macos`; with `nightly-2026-10-09` it builds either way.

nodes.body:
As it currently stands, Rhai loads an entire module including all of its functions, variables, etc when it is given to `Engine`. This is a lot of stuff to load, especially when most scripts will not use every function introduced into `Engine`. It is especially important in embedded contexts, where RAM is at a premium and nothing can go to waste.

Now, lazy loading allows `Engine` to only load specific items out of a `Module`. It will run top-level items, then registers the requested function/variable with the `Engine` for use. This function remains loaded for the lifetime of the `Engine` or until manually evicted. This feature is opt-in.

The way it works under the hood is creating a static registration table for each module that can be quickly searched for hot loading functions.
nodes.title: Lazy function loading

This is it.  The last piece of the puzzle.  A large PR in that.

This PR completely implements modules in Grain, including the ability to load Grain artifact modules from the AST walker, and vice versa.  Grain and script modules are completely interchangeable.

Missing features such as `export var`, `global::var`, and `path::to::func(...)` etc. all work seamlessly.

The `FileModuleResolver` defaults to try to load `.rgrn` files if it cannot find the corresponding `.rhai` files...

The pitfall is the introduction of a bunch of new opcodes, essentially the qualified versions of all the `CALL_FN` codes.  I don't see a way to avoid that unfortunately.

nodes.body:
Split out of #1178 as requested.

### Resolution misses for non-binary calls were never cached
In `resolve_fn`, once all `Dynamic` permutations are exhausted, the code returned `None` early for any call that does not have exactly two arguments. That return skipped the cache insert. The behaviour changed by accident in b0ce3ee4 (v1.10), when `or_insert_with` became an `Entry` match.

The result: a miss was only cached for binary calls. Before calling a native function, the evaluator checks whether a script function of the same name exists, using a lookup with no arguments. So that check never got cached. A call like `abs(x)` in a loop re-scanned every module for a script function on every iteration.

The fix keeps the built-in operator lookup restricted to two arguments (`args.filter(|_| num_args == 2)`) and lets every miss fall through to the cache insert. In #1178's benchmarks this made eager evaluation about 3–5% faster.

### The first resolution cache was dropped at the end of a block
Caches are created lazily. If the first one was created inside a block, such as a loop body, the block's `rewind_fn_resolution_caches` popped it at the end, so every iteration started with an empty cache. `eval_stmt_block` now pushes a cache before the block when none exists yet, so it lives for the rest of the evaluation. Popping a cache pushed for an `import` inside a block is unchanged.

### String interpolation
Each interpolated non-string value created a new `NativeCallContext`, which clones the global runtime state, and resolved `to_string` with fresh caches. The new `print_with_func_raw` resolves it through `exec_native_fn_call` with the evaluation's own `global` and `caches`. Both the AST interpreter and Rhai Grain use it.

### Tests
- `tests/functions.rs`: a native 1-argument call in a loop, alongside script functions with the same name and a different/the same arity.
- `tests/modules.rs`: global functions imported inside a block or a loop body don't leak past it (covers the cache-scoping change).
- `tests/string.rs`: interpolation with a custom `to_string`, in a loop and inside a function.

`cargo test --tests` passes with the default features and with `internals,grain`, `bin-features`, `no_function,no_module`, and `no_index,no_object,no_float`. Under that last set, `parse_json::test_parse_json_err_no_object` fails, but it fails the same way on `main`.

nodes.body:
## Purpose

This PR revamps the general handling of loops in the Grain VM.

## Why Loops Are Tricky

* They contain back-jumps that may lead to infinite loops, so they must _tick_ once in a while.
* They trap the `continue` and `break` keywords which breaks normal control flow.
* In Rhai, due to their flow-breaking nature, the `continue` and `break` keywords are implemented as _pseudo-errors_ (like `return` and `throw`); these pseudo-errors can potentially be returned from a function (e.g. in a custom syntax implementation).
* The compiler currently unwinds loops automatically, so this information is not strictly necessary except for `for` loops (which needs to keep track of the iterator object and the iteration count).
* Nevertheless, not knowing how many loops there are and where they are makes the implementation brittle.  In the future, when things happen deep inside loops, it becomes extremely troublesome to unwind properly.  This has occurred when enhancing the `switch` statement, and when implementing custom syntax, and will certainly occur again in the future with new language features.
* In the future when we want to add a tracing JIT, e.g., a tight loop would be the natural place to start and this info would again be needed.

## Limitations of The Original Implementation

* It only keeps information on `for` loops, omitting `while`, `loop` and `do` (because the compiler already lowers all of them).
* It ignores _pseudo-errors_ returned from functions (and other places), treating them all as normal errors.
* Some pseudo-errors (especially `continue` and `break`) needs to be revised to rewind loops.

## Current Revision

* A general `EnterLoop` opcode is introduced.  The `IterDrop` opcode is renamed `ExitLoop`.  They wrap each loop.
* `EnterLoop` does the work of `Tick`, so the `Tick` opcode is no longer used and deprecated.
* During runtime, loops are tracked on a stack, not just `for` loop iterators.  Therefore, `Vm::iterators` is renamed `Vm::Loops` and `Iteration` is renamed `Loop`.

## Impact

On  normal loops, they add four bytes to the payload (to hold the exit target), replacing the `Tick` op.

For reasonable loop lengths, the cost of added tracking is amortized over a large number of iterations, so impact is minimal.

The tracking involves pushing a `Loop` structure containing mostly `usize` fields.  Most of the counts would never exhaust a `usize`, possibly not even a `u8`. But let's leave them as `usize` unless profiling shows clear benefits in reducing the size of this struct.

For very short loops, such as repeatedly iterating loops with 1-2 iterations, which are quite rare, they still incur very small cost.
nodes.title: VM: Revamp loops handling

# Introduction

Custom syntax is a unique feature of Rhai, one used by many domain-specific applications to simplify code by providing new syntax suited to the domain usage.

# Grain Support
Previously, Grain rejects all custom syntax as fragments.  This PR adds support for custom syntax that does not touch the `scope`.

Custom syntax that touches the `scope`, like `eval`, remain non-lowerable. These cases are extremely rare.

# Implementation

Grain implements custom syntax via a new Opcode `Op::CustomSyntax` and a `custom_syntax` pool.

# `no_ast`

Finally, `no_ast` works with custom syntax, disabling only the parser half of it, but allows the execution part to work with Grain.
nodes.title: VM: Support Custom Syntax

nodes.body:
This PR replaces the unmaintained `smartstring` dependency with [`compact_str`](https://docs.rs/compact_str), which is actively maintained and also stores short strings inline (up to 24 bytes on 64-bit targets).

## Why

- **Unmaintained:** the `smartstring` repository was archived in May 2026, and RustSec published [RUSTSEC-2026-0249](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0249.html) for it. Every project that depends on Rhai is now flagged by `cargo deny check advisories` (an error with the default configuration) and by `cargo audit`. The only ways around it are an ignore entry or patching Rhai locally, and #1121 was opened for exactly that.
- **Soundness:** #816 reports unsoundness (possible UB) in `smartstring`, which Rhai uses for identifiers, map keys and `ImmutableString` internals. The proposed fix (bodil/smartstring#34) was never released, and now it never will be.
- **License:** `smartstring` is `MPL-2.0+`, while Rhai is `MIT OR Apache-2.0` (#897). `compact_str` is `MIT`, so Rhai's dependency tree becomes permissive again.
- **Same design:** `compact_str` offers the same inline small-string optimization for identifiers and map keys, supports `no_std` (`default-features = false`), and needed only one API change in Rhai (`new_const()` → `const_new("")`).

## Changes

- `type SmartString = compact_str::CompactString;` The aliases `Identifier` and the key type of `Map` follow.
- `SmartString::new_const()` / `Identifier::new_const()` → `const_new("")`. These are the only API differences Rhai used; nothing else in the interpreter changes.
- `compact_str = { version = ">=0.9, <0.11", default-features = false }`, with `std` wired to `compact_str/std`. No serde feature is needed, because Rhai no longer serializes `SmartString` directly (9e5a89df).
- MSRV stays at **1.66**. compact_str 0.10 requires Rust 1.71, so `Cargo.msrv.lock` pins 0.9.1 (plus `itoa 1.0.15`, the last version before 1.68). Regular builds get 0.10.
- `Cargo.msrv.lock` refresh is a separate commit. The lockfile still resolved rhai 1.21.0, so it is regenerated for the current manifest first. It was regenerated with `CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_RUST_VERSIONS=fallback cargo update -p rhai`, and `cargo +1.66.0 build` leaves it unchanged afterwards.
- CHANGELOG (1.27.0) and README dependency list updated.

## Compatibility

`rhai::Map` is public, so its key type changes from `SmartString<LazyCompact>` to `CompactString`. Code that uses `&str` lookups, `"key".into()` or `.as_str()` keeps compiling. Code that names `smartstring::SmartString` explicitly has to switch. The CHANGELOG lists this under *Potentially breaking changes*. If you would rather keep this for a 2.0 or behind a feature flag, I'm happy to rework it.

## Testing

Run locally against `main` (a6241621):

- `cargo test` for every flag set of the `build` matrix in `build.yml` (29 flag sets, 15,110 test executions in total), all green
- `cargo +1.66.0 build --features decimal,metadata,serde,debugging,grain` with `Cargo.msrv.lock`
- no_ast (3 flag sets), all 4 WASM builds (wasm32-wasip1, wasm32-unknown-unknown), i686 cross build
- `no_std/no_std_test` on nightly (`--profile unix`)
- `cargo +nightly fmt --all -- --check`, the CI clippy invocation, `cargo doc` with the CI feature set
- `codegen/tests/custom_root` tests. The `codegen` trybuild UI tests fail on `main` as well with current rustc (diagnostic wording changed). The set of failing UI files is identical with and without this PR.

Downstream, we already carry the same change on top of 1.25.1 via `[patch.crates-io]`.
nodes.title: Replace smartstring with compact str

nodes.body:
A very simple optimization for the `switch` statement.

Currently, a single `switch` statement lowers into two calls to `Op::Switch` -- one for the cases and one for the ranges.

In the predominant scenario of no range cases, there is no need to emit the dispatch to empty ranges.

This PR optimizes the lowering such that no second dispatch is emitted if there are no range cases.  It also saves the push and pop of the `Scope` by not storing the `switch` value.

Speed of the `switch` statement doubles to close to 2x the speed of the AST walker when there are no range cases.
nodes.title: VM: Double switch statement speed by not emitting the ranges dispatch if there are no range cases

nodes.body:
Currently, any loops (e.g. `for`, `while`, do`) emit a `()` with a `Pop` in the vast majority of cases where the loop's break value is not used.

This results with a push `()` followed by `Pop` for many loops.  Although most loops are long enough to make this immaterial, is it nevertheless not necessary.

This PR optimizes this with the `Lowered` return value just like for statement blocks.
nodes.title: VM: Optimize loops by not emitting a `()` if not needed.

nodes.body:
This PR speeds up chaining assignments such as `a[x] = something`.

Currently, the VM runs an assignment on a chain around 50% slower than the AST walker.

That is because it first calculates the resultant value, then pushes it into the `Scope` under a dummy name, then it processes the operands, and finally it reads the value back from the `Scope` and puts it back onto the stack.

This PR eliminates this entire process by changing the order of the stack pushes -- with the resultant value pushed first.  The whole process now operates purely on the stack without touching the `Scope`.

Chain assignments now run at par with the AST walker, with the `primes` bench reaching 1.0x speed.

Another minor enhancement is the use of `Scope::push_entry` which takes an `ImmutableString` which can be cloned from the strings interner.  This avoids additional allocations of the same strings over and over again.
nodes.title: VM: Speed up chaining assign.

Originally, Grain rolls its own indexing and property get/set logic.

Then indexing was rerouted to Rhai's standard `get_indexed_mut` function that properly handles a range of special situations, such as the `Engine::on_invalid_array_index` callback.

This PR routes also the property read/write process to Rhai, thus properly handling missing properties and the `Engine::on_map_missing_property` callback.

nodes.body:
Currently, when the `switch` statement is used, Grain requires fixing the hash seed due to Rhai's usage of hashing in the `switch` statement.  This is a limitation of the AST design, which throws away the original case value, keeping only the hash.

This PR adds back the constant value of each case for the `switch` statement into the AST, removing the need for Grain to store hashes in compiled bytecodes.

Now, the case values are stored as constants and the hashes are recalculated upon load.  Therefore, there is no need to probe the hashing seed and no need to check if they match.

The `HashSeedMismatch` error is deprecated (but left there for compatibility).

The bytecodes version is bumped due to the hash now replaced by a constant index.

Also, the cases are now stored in a `HashMap` instead of an array so linear search is avoided for very large `switch` statements.  Currently it does not appear to improve performance for general use cases.
nodes.title: VM: Simplify switch statement handling.
